title: Materials Around Us
description: Grade 6 Science: properties of materials — solubility, hardness, transparency, floating and sinking — and grouping and classifying materials. Notes, examples and a test.

topics.title: Materials and Their Properties
topics.concept:
Everything around us — a chair, a spoon, a window, your clothes — is made of some substance. The substance that a thing is made of is called its material. A single object can be made of more than one material (a pencil has wood and graphite), and the same material can be used to make many different objects (glass makes windows, bottles and bulbs).

We choose a material for a job based on its properties — the features that describe how it looks and behaves. Studying properties helps us understand why each material is used where it is.

  • Appearance — whether a material is shiny (lustrous) or dull. Metals like gold, silver and freshly cut iron are shiny; wood, chalk and paper are dull.
  • Hardness — materials that cannot be easily pressed, scratched or dented are hard (iron, stone, diamond); those that can be are soft (cotton, sponge, clay).
  • Rough or smooth — how the surface feels to the touch.

Because diamond is the hardest natural material, it is used to cut glass and other hard substances. Because iron is hard and strong, it is used to build gates and tools. Choosing the right property for the right use is the heart of this chapter.

examples.problem: Example 1: Give one example each of (a) a shiny material and (b) a dull material.
examples.solution:
Shiny (lustrous) materials reflect light; dull ones do not.

  • (a) Shiny — a metal such as silver or freshly cut iron.
  • (b) Dull — wood, chalk or paper.
examples.answer: (a) A metal such as silver is shiny; (b) wood or chalk is dull.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why is diamond used to cut glass?
examples.solution:
To cut a hard material you need an even harder one.

  • Diamond is the hardest natural material.
  • So it can scratch and cut glass, which is softer than diamond.
examples.answer: Because diamond is the hardest natural material, it can cut the softer glass.

examples.problem: Example 3: A pencil is made of two materials. Name them and the property that makes each suitable.
examples.solution:
A pencil combines materials with different useful properties.

  • Wood — light and easy to hold and sharpen.
  • Graphite (the ‘lead’) — soft and leaves a mark on paper.
examples.answer: Wood (light, easy to hold/sharpen) and graphite (soft, leaves a mark) — a single object made of two materials.

recap:
• The substance an object is made of is its material; one object may use several materials and one material may make many objects.
  • We pick materials by their properties: appearance (shiny/dull), hardness (hard/soft), rough/smooth.
  • Hard materials resist scratching and denting; soft ones do not.
  • The property decides the use — e.g. hard diamond cuts glass.

quiz.q: The substance that an object is made of is called its:
quiz.explanation: The substance an object is made of is its material.

quiz.q: Which property makes diamond suitable for cutting glass?
quiz.explanation: Diamond is the hardest natural material, so it can cut softer glass.

topics.title: Solubility, Transparency and Floating or Sinking
topics.concept:
Some properties of materials are best seen when we put them in water or hold them up to light.

Soluble and insoluble: A material that dissolves in water and seems to disappear is soluble (sugar, salt). One that does not dissolve is insoluble (sand, chalk powder). Liquids too can be soluble — lemon juice mixes fully with water (miscible), while oil does not and forms a separate layer (immiscible).

Floating and sinking: Some materials float on water (a piece of wood, a plastic bottle, a dry leaf) while others sink (a stone, an iron nail, a coin). Whether something floats or sinks depends on the material and its shape, not just its size.

Transparency: Based on how much light passes through them, materials are:

  • Transparent — you can see clearly through them; almost all light passes (clear glass, water, air).
  • Translucent — only some light passes, so things look blurred (butter paper, frosted glass, oiled paper).
  • Opaque — no light passes through, so you cannot see through them (wood, metal, cardboard, stone).

These properties decide everyday choices: windows use transparent glass to let in light, while a door uses opaque wood for privacy.

examples.problem: Example 1: Classify as soluble or insoluble in water: salt, sand, sugar, chalk powder.
examples.solution:
Soluble materials dissolve and seem to disappear; insoluble ones remain.

  • Soluble: salt, sugar.
  • Insoluble: sand, chalk powder.
examples.answer: Salt and sugar are soluble; sand and chalk powder are insoluble.

examples.problem: Example 2: Window glass and butter paper both let some light through. Which is transparent and which is translucent?
examples.solution:
Transparent lets you see clearly; translucent only lets light through in a blurred way.

  • Window glass — you can see clearly → transparent.
  • Butter paper — light passes but images are blurred → translucent.
examples.answer: Window glass is transparent; butter paper is translucent.

examples.problem: Example 3: Oil poured into water forms a separate layer instead of mixing. What do we call two such liquids?
examples.solution:
Liquids that do not mix stay in separate layers.

  • Oil and water do not mix together.
  • Such liquids are called immiscible.
examples.answer: They are called immiscible liquids (they do not mix).

recap:
• Soluble materials dissolve in water (sugar, salt); insoluble do not (sand, chalk).
  • Liquids that mix are miscible; those that do not are immiscible (oil and water).
  • Some materials float, others sink, depending on the material and shape.
  • Transparent (clear), translucent (blurred), opaque (no light through) describe how much light passes.

quiz.q: A material through which no light can pass is called:
quiz.explanation: Opaque materials do not allow any light to pass through them.

quiz.q: Which of these is soluble in water?
quiz.explanation: Sugar dissolves in water, so it is soluble; the others are insoluble.

topics.title: Grouping and Classification of Materials
topics.concept:
There are thousands of materials around us. To study and use them more easily, we group or classify them — that is, we put together materials that share a common property.

Grouping things is something we do all the time: a shopkeeper keeps all the soaps together and all the biscuits together; a library keeps science books on one shelf and story books on another. In science we group materials by a chosen property, for example:

  • By appearance — shiny materials in one group, dull in another.
  • By hardness — hard materials together, soft materials together.
  • By solubility — soluble together, insoluble together.
  • By transparency — transparent, translucent and opaque groups.

Why do we classify? Grouping makes it easier to find things, to study their properties together, and to choose the right material for a job. The same material can fall into different groups depending on the property we choose — glass is in the ‘hard’ group and also in the ‘transparent’ group. So the way we classify depends on the property we are interested in.

examples.problem: Example 1: Give two benefits of grouping materials.
examples.solution:
Classification organises a large number of materials.

  • It makes it easier to find and store things.
  • It helps us study similar materials together and pick the right one for a use.
examples.answer: Grouping makes materials easier to find/store and helps us study and choose them by their properties.

examples.problem: Example 2: Glass can be placed in the ‘hard’ group and also in the ‘transparent’ group. What does this show about classification?
examples.solution:
The group an object goes into depends on the chosen property.

  • By hardness, glass is hard.
  • By transparency, glass is transparent.
examples.answer: It shows the same material can belong to different groups depending on which property we use to classify.

examples.problem: Example 3: You are given: iron nail, sponge, sugar, sand, glass slab. Group them as soluble or insoluble in water.
examples.solution:
Test which dissolve in water.

  • Soluble: sugar.
  • Insoluble: iron nail, sponge, sand, glass slab.
examples.answer: Soluble: sugar. Insoluble: iron nail, sponge, sand and glass slab.

recap:
• Classification means grouping materials that share a property.
  • We can group by appearance, hardness, solubility or transparency.
  • Grouping helps us find, study and choose materials easily.
  • A material can belong to different groups depending on the property chosen.

quiz.q: Putting together materials that share a property is called:
quiz.explanation: Grouping materials by a shared property is classification.

quiz.q: The main reason we classify materials is to:
options: Make them easier to find, study and choose
quiz.explanation: Classification organises materials so they are easier to find, study and use.

questions.q: The substance an object is made of is called its:
questions.explanation: The substance an object is made of is its material.

questions.q: A feature that describes how a material looks or behaves is its:
questions.explanation: Properties describe how a material looks and behaves.

questions.q: Materials that shine are said to be:
questions.explanation: Shiny materials, like metals, are lustrous.

questions.q: Which of these is the hardest material?
questions.explanation: Diamond is the hardest known natural material.

questions.q: A material that dissolves in water is said to be:
questions.explanation: Soluble materials dissolve in water.

questions.q: Which of these is insoluble in water?
questions.explanation: Sand does not dissolve in water; it is insoluble.

questions.q: Oil and water do not mix. Such liquids are called:
questions.explanation: Liquids that do not mix are immiscible.

questions.q: Clear glass that you can see through is:
questions.explanation: Transparent materials let almost all light pass and you can see clearly.

questions.q: Butter paper, through which images look blurred, is:
questions.explanation: Translucent materials let only some light through, blurring images.

questions.q: Through which material can NO light pass?
questions.explanation: Wood is opaque; no light passes through it.

questions.q: Which is most likely to float on water?
questions.explanation: A dry wooden block floats; the dense metal and stone objects sink.

questions.q: Grouping materials that share a property is called:
questions.explanation: Grouping by a shared property is classification.

questions.q: We classify materials mainly to:
options: Find, study and choose them easily
questions.explanation: Classification organises materials so they are easier to use.

questions.q: Glass can be in the 'hard' group and the 'transparent' group. This shows a material can:
options: Belong to different groups by different properties
questions.explanation: The group depends on the property chosen, so one material can be in several groups.

questions.q: Windows are made of transparent glass mainly because it:
questions.explanation: Transparent glass lets daylight into the room.

questions.q: A spoonful of sugar is stirred into water until it disappears. The sugar has:
options: Dissolved and is still present in the water
questions.explanation: Dissolved sugar is still there (the water tastes sweet); it has not vanished.

questions.q: Two materials are tested: X lets you read print through it clearly, Y blurs the print but still lets light through. Then:
options: X is transparent, Y is translucent
X is opaque, Y is transparent
X is translucent, Y is transparent
questions.explanation: Clear viewing = transparent (X); blurred but lit = translucent (Y).

questions.q: A material is shiny, hard and opaque, and sinks in water. It is most likely a:
questions.explanation: Shiny, hard, opaque and dense (sinks) describes a metal.

questions.q: Why can the SAME material appear in more than one group when we classify?
options: Because the group depends on which property we choose
Because all materials are the same
questions.explanation: Different properties put a material into different groups (e.g. glass is hard and transparent).

questions.q: You must lift only the iron objects out of a mixture of iron nails, sugar and sand. The quickest way is to:
questions.explanation: A magnet attracts the iron nails, separating them quickly (using a property of the material).

questions.q: A ball of clay sinks, but the same clay shaped like a bowl floats. This shows that floating depends on:
options: The shape as well as the material
questions.explanation: The same material can float or sink depending on its shape.
